pathogen: Bipolaris maydis (Y. Nisik. & C. Miyake) Shoemaker

egypt_scope_and_evidence.egypt_evidence: A 2024 review of African maize foliar pathogens includes Egypt among countries where Bipolaris maydis-associated southern corn leaf blight has been reported. Egyptian literature also records Bipolaris-related fungi associated with maize and sorghum material.
egypt_scope_and_evidence.evidence_limit: A detailed Egypt-only survey of MLB incidence, regional prevalence, pathogen races, and yield losses was not located in the reviewed sources. The visual symptom description is therefore disease-specific, while Egypt-specific claims are kept separate and explicitly qualified.

early: Tiny yellow or pale chlorotic flecks
Small oval or water-soaked spots, commonly beginning on lower leaves
characteristic_leaf_lesions: Small diamond-shaped lesions that elongate with age
Elongated rectangular lesions constrained by adjacent leaf veins
Lesions may initially remain between veins and later merge
advanced: Coalescing lesions form large brown necrotic areas
Premature drying and death of leaves
Complete foliage blight in severe infections
Black or dark mould may appear on affected silks, husks, cobs, or kernels in severe/race-specific infections
image_annotation_targets: yellow flecks versus mature brown lesions
light centre and dark margin contrast
lesion coalescence and percentage of necrotic tissue
black mould on cob or husk when present

symptoms: possible black mould on husks, silks, cobs, or kernels
lesion_color: dark grey or black when sporulating/rotting

lesion_size.common_range: Approximately 3–22 mm long and 2–6 mm wide for typical early-to-mature leaf lesions
lesion_size.note: Lesion size and shape vary with the pathogen race, maize genotype, and disease severity.

distribution: Usually begins on lower leaves and increases upward through the canopy; severe disease can affect most foliage and, in some host-race combinations, above-ground reproductive tissues.
progression: Yellow flecks or small spots appear on lower leaves.
Spots enlarge into diamond-shaped tan or brown lesions.
Lesions elongate and become rectangular because growth is limited by leaf veins.
Lesions develop darker margins and may become dark grey or black when sporulation or secondary decay occurs.
Lesions merge, producing extensive necrosis, premature leaf death, and whole-leaf blighting.
Severe or race-specific infections may extend to husks, silks, ears, cobs, and kernels.

environment.humidity: High humidity; disease development is favoured by relative humidity above approximately 80%, with very prolonged leaf wetness especially favourable.
environment.temperature: Warm conditions, approximately 20–30 °C; some disease references report stronger development around 24–35 °C when foliage remains wet.
environment.leaf_wetness: Prolonged dew, rain, or irrigation wetness supports infection and sporulation.
environment.egypt_interpretation: These conditions can occur in Egyptian maize production, but the reviewed sources did not provide an Egypt-specific temperature or humidity threshold study.
environment.spread: Conidia are dispersed mainly by wind and rain splash; infected residue can provide inoculum.

pathogen_race_note.egypt_specific_race: Not established from the Egypt-specific sources reviewed.
pathogen_race_note.visual_relevance: Race O generally causes smaller, vein-limited leaf lesions. Race T can cause larger lesions with chlorotic halos and may involve sheaths, husks, ears, and cobs on susceptible T-cytoplasm maize.

similar_diseases.name: Northern Leaf Blight
similar_diseases.visual_difference: Long grey-green to tan cigar-shaped lesions, often several centimetres long, rather than the smaller diamond-to-rectangular lesions of MLB.

similar_diseases.name: Gray Leaf Spot
similar_diseases.visual_difference: Usually narrow grey or tan rectangular lesions that are strongly vein-limited and less distinctly brown-margined.

similar_diseases.name: Common Rust
similar_diseases.visual_difference: Raised orange-brown pustules are the principal visible sign, not flat diamond-shaped necrotic lesions.

recommended_image_search_terms: Bipolaris maydis maize Egypt leaf lesions
southern corn leaf blight Egypt diamond lesions
maize MLB rectangular brown lesions lower leaves
diagnostic_caution: Visual identification is suggestive, not definitive. Confirm doubtful cases through microscopy of conidia, fungal isolation, or molecular testing, particularly when Northern Leaf Blight or Gray Leaf Spot is also present.

research_notes: MLB and Southern Corn Leaf Blight refer to the same maize disease caused by Bipolaris maydis. This record is optimized for visual image annotation and preserves the distinction between Egypt-specific evidence and general disease biology.
